\subsection{Transfer-learning protocol}
\label{sec:sota-protocol}

Two pretrained architectures were adapted to EuroSAT:
MobileNetV2~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2}, and EfficientNet-B0~\cite{tan2019efficientnet}.
Both are initialized with ImageNet weights and the final linear layer of each classifier was replaced by a
new ten-class prediction layer. Every run uses the same stratified split as the Models A and B, 
random seed, augmentation, training-split normalization statistics, batch
size of 128, 30-epoch budget and Colab Tesla~T4 as the machine to run on. 
The checkpoint was chosen by lowest validation loss, before testing.

After adding the new prediction layer, there were two cases to choose from, either
keep the pretrained backbone \emph{frozen}, or \emph{fine-tune} it. Each
network was tested with using both methods, to decide wether there is a gain by fine tuning all parameters.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Frozen.} In this case, only the new prediction layer was trained, with Adam Optimizer at
  a learning rate of $10^{-3}$. The CNN backbone was used as a fixed feature extractor,
  with its batch-normalisation statistics held at their original ImageNet values.
  \item \textbf{Fine-tuned.} In this case, every weight was trained, starting from the
  ImageNet weights, with Adam using a learning rate of $10^{-4}$. Here we chose a smaller learning rate
 than the frozen-backbone rate to limit changes to the pretrained filters while
  the new classifier learns.
\end{itemize}

Our main runs keep the input at  the original resolution that the custom
models see, which is $64\times64$. Because ImageNet networks are
designed for $224\times224$ input, the experiment was repeated for each network
with the $64\times64$ images upsampled to $224\times224$, for both the frozen and fine-tuned cases. Each $224\times224$
pair differs from its original pair in input size only, so as to identify the effect of keeping the input images at the original resolution that the pretrained networks were trained on.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:sota-results}

  \centering

  \footnotesize
  \setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
  \generatedtable{tables/sota_comparison.tex}{\#22}
  \caption{Pretrained lightweight models on the EuroSAT test split. Precision
  and recall are averages over the ten classes. \emph{Trained} counts the
  parameters updated during training. Sizes are in MB, measured from the saved
  weights; the custom models in Table~\ref{tab:custom-comparison} are in KB.
  The rows under Supplementary section upsamples the $64\times64$ images to $224\times224$.}

Table~\ref{tab:sota-comparison} shows results obtained with both the frozen and fine-tuned configurations for each of the two networks.\emph{Parameters} and \emph{Size} are
the same for the frozen and fine-tuned runs of the same network. Freezing a configuration
only changes which parameters are trained, and threfore the difference is in the \emph{Trained} column. Accuracy
gaps between the two rows of a pair is therefore obtained with training effort
only, with no costs in the saved model's size. Fine-tuning does need more memory
during training, because gradients are computed for every layer.

We observed that for both networks that accuracy gap is large. Fine-tuning raises all the metrics by well
above the frozen feature extractor CNN case. The likely explanation is the domain shift from ImageNet to Satellite Images.
ImageNet filters were learnt on close-range photographs of objects, while
EuroSAT is overhead satellite images at a much smaller scale. 
A frozen backbone can only re-weight features learnt for the wrong kind of image, and a fine-tuned configuration can let the filters evolve to field boundaries, road textures and water.

Frozen, EfficientNet-B0 was found to be the weaker network, despite having almost twice
MobileNetV2's parameters. In the Fine-tuned case, the two networks are almost at the same level. The
gap between the frozen runs shows how well each network's learned ImageNet features happen to
transfer to $64\times64$ satellite images.
Once MobileNetV2 is fine-tuned, it is clearly the better edge candidate of the two.

The supplementary rows show that increasing the resolution from $64\times64$ to $224\times224$ gives both frozen backbones a gain of
few additional points, but the fine-tuned models gain less than one point. A possible explanation for this is the fact that frozen
network's filters are designed to fit ImageNet's scale, so upsampling the input
is the only way to bring the data to them. Instead, fine-tuning moves the
filters to the data, after which resolution becomes less important. For each of the two
networks, the fine-tuned $64\times64$ model outperforms the frozen
$224\times224$ one. It also does about $(224/64)^2\approx12$ times fewer
operations per image, because a convolution layers cost depends on the $H\times W$
of its output. For an edge device,
fine-tuning at native resolution is the cheaper way to get accuracy.

Even the smallest of these models is one to two orders of magnitude larger than Model~B (Table~\ref{tab:custom-comparison}). Whether the additional accuracy is worth that storage is the
question Section~\ref{sec:task6} answers.

The training curves (Figures~\ref{fig:sota-loss}--\ref{fig:efficientnet-224-loss})
show the difference between the two approaches for both networks. Each frozen
run converges at a higher loss than its respective fine-tuned one. The frozen
EfficientNet-B0 curves are also visibly noisier than MobileNetV2's. After the
first few epochs both of its losses fluctuate without converging, and at $224\times224$ the lowest validation loss happens to fall early,
so its selected checkpoint comes early in the run. Meanwhile, the fine-tuned curves of
both networks are smooth and settle within a few epochs.

The noise in the frozen EfficientNet-B0 curves appears only when the feature extraction is fixed. Whereas its validation loss oscillates from epoch to
epoch, its validation accuracy changes much less. This suggests that the predicted classes
barely change and that what changes is mainly the confidence given to the images that
the frozen feature layers are unable to separate, although the saved histories
contain no per-image predictions to confirm it. Cross-entropy heavily penalises a confidently
wrong prediction, so small updates to the prediction layer move the
loss on these borderline images much more than they move the accuracy.
MobileNetV2's frozen features have fewer misclassified images, and its loss is lower
and more stable. The two backbones also terminate in different activation functions.
EfficientNet-B0 uses the unbounded SiLU
activation function~\cite{tan2019efficientnet}, and a small fraction of images produce
very large pooled features. 
MobileNetV2's ReLU6 activation limits each feature at
six~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2}. This bounded behaviour is discussed in
Section~\ref{sec:activation-choice}. In a diagnostic check which retrained only the prediction
layer (committed as \texttt{results/frozen\_head\_diagnostic}), normalizing those
features reduced the fluctuation but did not remove it.
Using different learning rates of $3\times10^{-4}$ and $10^{-4}$
did not remove it either, so neither the feature scale nor the learning rate
alone explains it.
The practical impact is in checkpoint selection. On a noisy validation curve
the lowest-loss epoch is partly random, and it need not be the
epoch with the best accuracy. Fine-tuning removes this effect, likely because the backbone
adapts its features to EuroSAT, which is another reason the comparison in
Section~\ref{sec:task6} uses the fine-tuned runs.

The confusion matrices of the fine-tuned $64\times64$ models
(Figures~\ref{fig:mobilenetv2-confusion} and~\ref{fig:efficientnet-confusion})
identify the errors in the same few class pairs for both networks.
Highway and River are confused in both directions, possibly due to the fact thatat $64\times64$ both are
thin line features a few pixels wide. There is also a substantial number of errors for the agricultural and vegetation
classes(AnnualCrop, PermanentCrop, Pasture and HerbaceousVegetation).
